reference: Daskin, M. S. "Network and Discrete Location: Models, Algorithms, and Applications." Wiley (1995).
math_formula:
### Mathematical Model
A compact multi-commodity distribution network has commodities C, product plants P, candidate distribution centers D, and customer zones Z. Continuous variable Shipped[c,p,d,z] is the amount of commodity c shipped from plant p through distribution center d to zone z. Binary variable Selected[d] indicates whether distribution center d is opened. Binary variable Served[d,z] indicates whether zone z is assigned to distribution center d. Minimize variable shipping cost plus fixed distribution-center selection cost plus unit throughput cost on assigned zone demand. Supply constraints limit sum_{d,z} Shipped[c,p,d,z] by Supply[c,p]. Served-demand constraints require sum_p Shipped[c,p,d,z] = Demand[c,z] Served[d,z]. Each zone is assigned to exactly one distribution center. Explicit open-before-assignment constraints require Served[d,z] <= Selected[d]. Throughput constraints enforce MinThroughput[d] Selected[d] <= sum_{c,z} Demand[c,z] Served[d,z] <= MaxThroughput[d] Selected[d]. A facility-limit policy prevents all centers from opening in small generated instances.
natural_language_example: A distribution planner chooses which candidate distribution centers to operate and assigns each customer zone to exactly one open center. Multiple commodities can be shipped from product plants through the selected centers to customer zones. Each plant has commodity-specific supply, each zone has commodity-specific demand, each center has a fixed opening cost, unit throughput cost, and minimum and maximum throughput if opened, and each commodity-plant-center-zone lane has a variable shipping cost. The goal is to minimize total distribution cost while satisfying assigned demand exactly and respecting supply, open-before-assignment, and throughput limits.
